items.prompt: Two mechanics disagree and you cannot check a car yourself. What can you use instead of a coin flip?
choices: Signals such as incentive, track record, specificity and consensus
Whichever mechanic sounds more sure of themselves, since certainty shows skill
Whichever quote is cheaper, since a lower price is the more honest one
items.explanation: Credibility signals are information short of checking the claim yourself. They turn a coin flip into an informed bet.

items.prompt: Is credibility a single yes-or-no property a person either has or lacks?
choices: Yes, a person either has it or lacks it, with nothing in between
No, it is built from several signals that can disagree
Yes, a job title settles it once and for all
items.explanation: Credibility is built from separate signals, and one person can score well on one and badly on another.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a credibility signal?
choices: How confident the speaker sounds
Whether the speaker gains if you believe them
Whether the speaker named a checkable cause
items.explanation: Confidence is cheap to produce and easy to fake, so it is not one of the signals.

items.prompt: What is the realistic goal of weighing credibility?
choices: Proof of which expert is right
A trick that always reveals the truth with no expertise
A better-informed bet than a coin flip
items.explanation: Without expertise of your own you cannot reach proof. You can shift the odds.

items.prompt: One signal looks bad for a claim. Is the claim automatically dismissed?
choices: Yes, one bad signal is decisive
No, each signal can mislead when used alone
Yes, any single weak signal ends the question
items.explanation: Every signal can mislead in isolation, which is why they are combined.

items.prompt: How many credibility signals does this unit name?
choices: Five: incentive, track record, specificity, consensus and recency
Two: how much the repair costs and how sure the speaker sounds about it
Three: job title, tone of voice and how old the speaker is
items.explanation: The five signals are incentive, track record, specificity, consensus and recency.

items.prompt: After weighing the signals, what do you end up with?
choices: A verified fact about the car
A ranking of the mechanics that cannot be wrong
A more informed bet, not a certainty
items.explanation: The process shifts the odds. Only checking the car itself gives certainty.

items.prompt: Why is asking a mechanic "are you sure?" weak evidence?
choices: Confidence is cheap to produce and easy to fake
Mechanics never answer a question like that directly
A sure answer always means the diagnosis is wrong
items.explanation: Sounding certain costs nothing, so it tells you little about being right.

items.prompt: A review says Mechanic B "seems honest and speaks with total certainty." Which credibility signals has the review actually supplied?
choices: Track record, because the review says he is honest in general
Specificity, because it describes how he spoke in detail
None of them, because tone and impression are not signals
Consensus, because a reviewer agreed with what he said
items.explanation: The review gives impression and confidence. A track-record signal would cite a specific, checkable past diagnosis.
items.reference:
Five signals, none decisive alone
🪙 Incentive: what do they gain if I believe them?
📋 Track record: right before, in checkable ways?
🔎 Specificity: did they name a checkable cause?
🤝 Consensus: do independent sources agree?
🕒 Recency: does this kind of claim go stale?
Why: no single signal settles a disagreement, so credibility comes from combining them into a better bet.
items.learnMore:
Credibility is a set of signals

Each signal answers a different question about a claim. They can disagree about the same person, so the useful move is to read all of them and bet, not to hunt for one that settles it.

Common mistake

Treating confident delivery as one of the signals.

items.prompt: What is an incentive check?
choices: Asking whether the speaker has ever told a lie before
Asking how many years they have worked
Asking what the speaker gains if you believe them
items.explanation: It is about their stake in your belief, not a judgment of their honesty.

items.prompt: Does having an incentive mean a person is lying?
choices: No, it lowers the weight of the claim on its own
Yes, any stake in the answer means the claim is false
Yes, a stake proves the speaker is being dishonest
items.explanation: An incentive gives an honest mistake a consistent direction. It does not prove dishonesty.

items.prompt: A mechanic who earns from brake jobs says it is the brakes. Where does their incentive point?
choices: Toward finding no problems
Toward the cheapest possible repair
Toward finding brake problems
items.explanation: Their income grows when brake work is needed, so honest errors tend to lean that way.

items.prompt: Which source has the weakest stake in what you decide?
choices: A salesperson who is paid for every sale
A neutral inspector paid a flat fee
A shop that earns money from the repair
items.explanation: A flat-fee inspector gains nothing from either answer.

items.prompt: A diagnosis runs against the speaker's own financial interest. What does that suggest?
choices: A modest point in its favor
Conclusive proof that it must be true
A small point against it
items.explanation: Claims against interest are somewhat more believable, but they are not proof.

items.prompt: Should you ignore every source that has an incentive?
choices: Yes, interested sources are out
Yes, drop them unless they offer a discount
No, weigh their claim lower instead
items.explanation: An interested claim is a weaker input, not a worthless one.

items.prompt: Which of these is an incentive question?
choices: How loud and fast is the speaker talking?
Who profits if I act on this?
How long was their answer?
items.explanation: Incentive is about who benefits from your belief.

items.prompt: A friend who sells solar panels says your roof suits solar. What is the sensible reading?
choices: Worthless, since they sell the panels themselves
Reliable, because friends are always honest with us
A weaker input that needs other signals behind it
items.explanation: Their claim still counts, but it carries less weight than a neutral source's.

items.prompt: Two sources both say a repair is needed: the shop that would do it, and an inspector paid a flat fee whatever they find. How does the incentive check treat them?
choices: The shop's claim is dropped because it earns from the repair
The inspector's view is stronger, but the shop's still counts
Both count equally because both examined the same car
The inspector's claim is dropped because inspectors miss repairs
items.explanation: Neutrality makes the inspector's view stronger evidence. It does not turn the shop's claim into zero.
items.reference:
Whose answer pays?
🔧 Shop that does the repair: gains if you say yes
🧾 Inspector paid a flat fee: gains either way
📉 Claim against own interest: small plus
⚖️ Interest lowers weight, it does not erase it
Why: an incentive gives honest errors a consistent direction, so the claim deserves less weight alone, not zero.
items.learnMore:
The incentive check lowers weight, it does not accuse

Someone who profits from a particular answer will tend, even honestly, to lean toward it. Ask who gains and by how much, then give the claim less weight on its own, not none.

Dismissing an interested source entirely, or treating a neutral source as automatically right.

items.prompt: A forecast gives a time window and a chance of rain. Compared with a repeated "rain tomorrow," it is...

Less useful, because it might turn out to be wrong
The same thing, because both of them predict rain tomorrow
items.explanation: A claim that can miss is a claim you can learn from.

items.prompt: Why are vague claims hard to test?

They can be read as correct after the fact
They are always false once somebody examines them
items.explanation: A vague claim stretches to fit whatever happens.

items.prompt: One forecaster says "cold front around 2pm, 60% chance of rain between 1 and 4pm." Another repeats "definitely rain, I'm sure." Why is the first more useful before tomorrow arrives?
choices: It states in advance what would count as right or as wrong
It is more likely to be correct because it has more words
It shows the forecaster has worked at the station longer
It proves rain will fall during the afternoon window given
items.explanation: Specificity lets you judge the claim against what actually happens. Detail alone proves nothing.

items.explanation: Software changes quickly. Arithmetic and settled physics do not.

items.explanation: A one-day-old diagnosis of the same unchanged car is still current.

items.prompt: Is a newer claim always better?

Yes, a newer source always wins out

items.explanation: In a stable field, newer adds nothing.

items.prompt: Which old claim most needs rechecking before you rely on it?

🩺 Medical guidance: can be superseded

items.explanation: Chance rarely lines up several separate errors.

items.prompt: Why is Mechanic C's agreement worth more than Mechanic A repeating their own diagnosis?
choices: C is cheaper, and cheaper opinions are more honest overall
C sounded more confident than A during the conversation
C is a separate person with a separate stake, asked cold
C and A both examined the same car in the same week
items.explanation: Independence, not count or confidence, is what gives agreement its weight.
items.reference:
Repeated versus independent
🔁 A says "brakes" twice: one voice, one stake
🆕 C says "heat shield" cold: new person, new stake
👂 Told the others first: no longer independent
🧾 Fee-only assessor: stake removed
Why: independent agreement is hard to produce by accident, while a repeated claim is only one voice again.
items.learnMore:
Independence is what gives consensus its weight

Counting voices is not enough. Agreement matters when the people are separate, hold different stakes and have not heard each other. Otherwise a crowd can simply share one bias.

Common mistake

Treating majority as proof, or asking a new mechanic after sharing earlier opinions.
items.reflection: Think of a decision where everyone you asked agreed. Had they heard each other, and did they share the same stake?

items.prompt: A fourth mechanic is told "two said heat shield, one said brakes" before inspecting. Why is their agreement weak?
choices: Fourth opinions are always weaker than the first three
They heard the others first, so it is no longer independent
Telling them the opinions makes them more likely to be wrong
They would be paid for the repair, which cancels everything
items.explanation: Prior exposure contaminates the signal that made an independent match meaningful.

items.prompt: All three mechanics, each paid for the repair, say the expensive brake diagnosis. What does consensus alone tell you?
choices: The brake diagnosis is confirmed because three outweigh one
Real agreement, but a shared stake makes independence partial
The consensus is worthless because all three earn from repairs
The cheaper dissenting view must be wrong since it is outnumbered
items.explanation: Shared incentives weaken independence. Consensus must be read together with the other signals.

items.prompt: Which step best buys back independence when every shop profits from the same repair?
choices: Ask a fourth shop that does the repair for a quote
Ask a shop that will not do the repair to show the part
Ask the first shop again with a more detailed question
Ask the most confident shop to put its claim in writing
items.explanation: Changing who benefits, and asking for something checkable, restores what a bigger crowd cannot.
